papers.title: The Para-ISS Dural Space Enhancement Sign: A Novel MRI Finding Independently Associated With Intracranial Atherosclerotic Burden
papers.abstract: Background: No dural enhancement sign centered on the inferior sagittal sinus (ISS) has been characterized. We observed a frequent, previously undescribed finding - para-ISS dural space enhancement (PISE) - at the free inferior margin of the falx cerebri. Objective: To define PISE, determine its detection rate in a large cross-sectional cohort, and characterize its correlates, in particular whether the pattern of association is compatible with an atherosclerosis-related dural mechanism. Methods: Consecutive contrast-enhanced intracranial vessel-wall MRI (VWI) examinations (May 2015-December 2025) were reviewed; 835 of 875 examinations were evaluable, corresponding to 811 patients. The first outcome-evaluable examination for each patient was used for all primary analyses. PISE was defined as dural enhancement strictly at the falx free margin adjacent to the ISS, exceeding the ISS vascular lumen. Forty-seven demographic, clinical-history, and imaging variables were tested univariately with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction; multivariable logistic regression with patient-grouped 5-fold cross-validation was triangulated with LASSO and random forest. Dose-response across plaque grades was assessed with the Cochran-Armitage trend test, and circulation-specific associations were compared in models adjusted for age and sex (inter-reader Cohen's kappa = 0.93). Results: PISE was detected in 609/811 patients (75.1%); detection rose from 50.0% ( 70 years; trend p = 5.6 x 10^-6). The strongest univariate correlate was vulnerable intracranial plaque (OR=8.29, 95% CI 5.54-12.40). Detection increased across plaque grades 0/1/2 (38.7% -> 77.2% -> 90.3%; Z=11.09). Anterior-circulation plaque showed a stronger association than posterior-circulation plaque (OR=4.42 vs 2.76). Vulnerable plaque (OR=2.37), plaque grade (OR=2.84 per grade), age (OR=1.38 per SD), and inpatient status (OR=3.18) remained independently associated (patient-grouped cross-validated AUC=0.755). Moyamoya disease was inversely associated (OR=0.25). Findings were consistent across imputation and all-examination sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: PISE is a frequently detected novel dural enhancement sign whose independent, graded, anatomically concordant association with intracranial atherosclerotic burden supports an atherosclerosis-related dural mechanism and warrants prospective validation.

papers.title: Similar discrimination, different behaviour under synthetic occlusion: confidence and attribution reproducibility of deep learning models for intraoral ultrasonography
papers.abstract: Objectives: To determine whether similar baseline discrimination conceals different responses to synthetic occlusion, whether loss of discrimination is accompanied by reduced confidence, and whether spatial attributions are reproducible in intraoral ultrasonography models. Methods: We analysed 477 images from 40 healthy volunteers, using acquisition position to label superior and inferior subregions. Five architectures were evaluated across five training seeds on a subject-independent test set of 97 images from eight volunteers. Images underwent constant-intensity occlusion at boundaries spanning 30-70% of image depth and an area-matched band-occlusion control. Attribution analyses assessed variation across seeds and class-activation methods and compared attribution-guided insertion with random insertion. Results: Seed-mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.958 to 0.972, with rankings reversing across seeds. EfficientNet-B0 fell below 0.60 in 49 of 50 boundary-sweep conditions, compared with zero to two for the other architectures; the difference persisted with area-matched masking. Under 50% occlusion, its mean confidence on incorrect predictions rose to 0.989 and expected calibration error from 0.094 to 0.478. Between two inference runs, EfficientNet-B0's per-seed occluded AUCs differed by up to 0.161; seed means were 0.51-0.55 in both. Attribution patterns varied across seeds and methods.

papers.title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort
papers.abstract: Objective: We aimed to 1) evaluate whether AI algorithms could identify a very low-risk sub-population Lung-RADS 1/2 cases suitable for a safe switch to biennial screening, and 2) externally validate Sybil, an imaging-based deep learning lung cancer risk prediction tool. Materials and methods: We gathered all lung cancer screenings (LCSs) from a tertiary safety-net hospital (n=3120, up to September 2024), manually extracted relevant clinical data, and analyzed Sybil's performance across various subgroups, with a specific focus on Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases. We simulated LCS interval extension using Sybil and the Brock model risk scores calibrated on a subset of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. Results: The median follow-up was 2.3 years (interquartile range 1.5-3.1), with a total 6-year cancer incidence rate of 2.3% (72/3120). Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases comprised 90.5% of our scans. Sybil's overall area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.819 to 0.912; while its 2-year AUC for Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases was 0.746. In the screening interval extension simulation, calibrating for a 30% shift to biennial screening translated into 33.8% of negative screens in our data being safely extended using Sybil, with no delayed cancers. The Brock model demonstrated an AUC of 0.513 on our data, with a sensitivity of 18.2% using the 1.5% threshold. Conclusion: Sybil has the potential to safely extend LCS intervals for low-risk individuals, reducing radiology workload and opening spots for life-saving new screenings.

papers.title: AI-Based MRI Radiomics for Preoperative Detection of Tumor Deposits in Rectal Cancer: A Bivariate Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Background: In rectal cancer (RC), tumor deposits (TDs) are clinically important as they are associated with a negative impact on prognosis and affect risk stratification as well as management plans. MRI radiomics combined with artificial intelligence (AI) has been explored for non-invasive preoperative TDs detection. However, results vary across studies; therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool their diagnostic test accuracy (DTA). Methods: This systematic review and DTA meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy and reported in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA). Databases were screened for DTA studies of MRI-based radiomics predicting TDs in adult RC patients with histopathology as reference. Results: Nine studies (2589 patients) were identified. Across included studies, the bivariate meta-analysis showed pooled sensitivity of 0.765 (95% CI 0.714 - 0.809) and specificity of 0.790 (95% CI 0.750 - 0.825), with overall AUC of 0.845 and very low heterogeneity (I2 = 7.3%). In validation datasets, diagnostic performance remained consistent (AUC 0.806), with pooled sensitivity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809) and specificity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809). For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p[≥]0.192). Models combining radiomics with clinical/radiological variables achieved significantly higher sensitivity (0.842 vs 0.657, p<0.001) and higher AUC (0.827 vs 0.752), with comparable specificity. Conclusion: MRI-based radiomics demonstrates good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in RC. The integration of radiomics with clinical or imaging features increases the accuracy of identification. Amongst the MRI modalities, models that utilize the combination of T2WI plus DWI are more accurate than those using T2WI or DWI only.

papers.title: Fibromuscular Dysplasia in Acute Type A Aortic Dissection: A Common yet Underrecognized Vascular Phenotype in Women
papers.abstract: Objectives: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non inflammatory, non atherosclerotic arterial disease characterized by multifocal arterial beading that predominantly affects women. Although FMD commonly involves the renal and carotid arteries, its relationship with acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) remains poorly understood. We investigated the proportion of patients with FMD among patients with ATAAD, focusing on sex based differences. Materials and Methods: Patients aged below 70 years with ATAAD and ECG triggered aortic CT angiography (CTA) were consecutively included in this retrospective single-center study. FMD was defined as multifocal arterial beading (string-of-beads appearance) in at least one vascular territory, according to international consensus criteria. The highest-quality CTA examination was evaluated by an experienced cardiovascular radiologist. All suspected FMD cases were independently reviewed by a second experienced cardiovascular radiologist, with the final diagnosis established by consensus. Proportions were reported with 95% confidence intervals and compared between sexes . Results: Of 214 patients screened, 200 were included (138 men and 62 women). FMD was confirmed in 18/200 patients (9%; 95% CI, 6 till 14%), none of whom had a prior FMD diagnosis. FMD was more frequent in women (12/62, 19%; 95% CI, 11 till 31%) than men (6/138, 4%; 95% CI, 2 till 9%; P<0.001). FMD predominantly involved the renal arteries. Additional carotid CTA was available in 49/200 patients (25%) and in 7/18 patients with FMD (39%); three of these seven patients had carotid FMD. Conclusion: FMD was observed in a substantial proportion of patients presenting with ATAAD, particularly women. These findings suggest that FMD is an underrecognized vascular phenotype in patients with ATAAD.

papers.title: PROSPECTIVE COMPARISON OF OPTIMIZED COMPRESSED SENSING AND GRAPPA-ACCELERATED 3D-TOF-MRA FOR EVALUATION OF UNTREATED INTRACRANIAL ANEURYSMS AT 1.5 T: A NON-INFERIORITY STUDY
papers.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES 3D-TOF-MRA is a standard non-invasive method for detecting and monitoring intracranial aneurysms, but long scan times remain a limitation. Compressed sensing (CS) acceleration for intracranial aneurysm evaluation has mainly been studied at 3T. This prospective single-center non-inferiority study compared CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T with GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF-MRA for evaluating untreated intracranial aneurysms. MATERIALS AND METHODS Sample size was determined via a preliminary retrospective study. 25 patients with 32 untreated aneurysms underwent both CS- (factor 7, 3:04 min) and GRAPPA-accelerated (factor 2, 5:00 min) 3D-TOF, yielding a 38.7% scan-time reduction. Two blinded neuroradiologists assessed overall image quality (primary endpoint) and artifacts, subjective CNR, aneurysm delineation and diameters (secondary endpoints). Non-inferiority was tested via one-sided t-test (prespecified 10% margin); interrater agreement used ICC. RESULTS CS demonstrated non-inferiority to GRAPPA for overall image quality in both readers (p <= .023), though interrater agreement was low (ICC 0.241-0.262), reflecting subjective variability. Secondary exploratory analyses showed heterogeneous preferences. ROI-based CNR was lower for CS (median 169.6; IQR, 91.0-226. vs. 278.2; 181.0-366.2). Aneurysm diameter measurements showed excellent interrater agreement for both techniques (CS ICC, 0.899-0.980; GRAPPA ICC, 0.877-0.973; all p < .001). CONCLUSION CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T met non-inferiority criteria vs. GRAPPA-TOF for overall image quality, reducing scan time by 38.7% while preserving aneurysm measurement reliability. However, reduced CNR and reader-preference variability important trade-offs.

papers.title: ACCURACY OF COMPRESSED SENSING ACCELERATED 3D-FLAIR IN THE DIAGNOSTIC WORK-UP OF MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS AT 1.5 T
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND3D-FLAIR is central to MR-based diagnosis and monitoring of MS, but long acquisition times remain a limitation. OBJECTIVESThis single-center prospective non-inferiority study evaluated whether compressed sensing (CS) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR at 1.5T provides lesion detection comparable to optimized Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition (GRAPPA) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR. Optimized CS- and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR sequences were incorporated into MRI examinations in patients with known or suspected MS. The primary endpoint was manual lesion count by two blinded readers using a 10% non-inferiority margin. Secondary endpoints included image quality, SNR, CNR, and automated lesion count and volumetry. RESULTSSixty-eight patients were included (mean age, 40.1{+/-}13.3 years; 61.8% women). CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR reduced acquisition time by 31.8% compared with GRAPPA (4:00 vs 5:52 minutes). Non-inferiority for manual lesion count was demonstrated for both readers (reader A, p < .0001; reader B, p = .005). Interrater agreement was excellent for CS (ICC = 0.921; 95% CI, 0.837-0.957) and very good for GRAPPA (ICC = 0.851; 95% CI, 0.769-0.906). Subjective image quality was high for both techniques. GRAPPA showed higher objective signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise-ratio (CNR), whereas automated lesion counts and volumes were higher for CS. CONCLUSIONCS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR provided non-inferior lesion detection with substantial scan-time reduction.

papers.title: Real-time Volumetric Imaging for Minimally-Invasive Thoracic Interventions: A Deformable Phantom Study
papers.abstract: ObjectivesThis study aimed to evaluate the ability of VoxelMap, a deep learning framework for 3D respiratory motion estimation, to generate volumetric images in real-time from 2D projections acquired for two deformable lung phantoms on a clinical interventional C-arm angiography system. Materials and MethodsVoxelMap was evaluated using the PixelPrint4D and Casper deformable physical thoracic respiratory phantoms. Four-dimensional cone-beam CT (4D CBCT) images acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system were used for network training and volumetric ground truth. Prediction accuracy was evaluated on withheld respiratory phases using structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). Model inference time was measured to assess suitability for continuous real-time processing. Deep ensembles were also used to assess model uncertainty. Correlation between ensemble uncertainty and prediction error was evaluated for both phantoms. ResultsVoxelMap achieved high prediction accuracy across withheld respiratory phases in both physical phantoms. SSIM values exceeded 0.92 in all experiments, with a higher performance observed for the Casper phantom (0.969-0.973) than for the PixelPrint4D phantom (0.927-0.943). Model inference times were less than 15 ms for both phantoms which is compatible with real-time processing. Ensemble uncertainty was positively correlated with prediction error in both phantoms, indicating that higher uncertainty was associated with less accurate volumetric predictions. ConclusionsOur study demonstrated that VoxelMap generates accurate volumetric deformations of respiratory anatomy from projections acquired on a clinical interventional C-arm system, with computational inference times compatible with continuous processing. By deriving volumetric information directly from two-dimensional fluoroscopic projections, VoxelMap has the potential to augment continuous fluoroscopic guidance with continuously updated volumetric information. Ensemble uncertainty may provide a potentially useful indicator of prediction reliability. Further studies using clinically representative training data and patient studies is required to establish clinical utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/Image-X-Institute/Voxelmap.

papers.title: Repeatability and reproducibility of spectral results with clinical photon-counting CT: multi-center phantom study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPhoton-counting CT utilizes a new detector technology that enhances quantitative imaging but introduces new system sensitivities that may affect quantitative reproducibility. For biomarkers, this quantitative reproducibility across protocol parameters, between institutions, and over time boosts their generalizability and clinical adoption for improved disease stratification. While stability across protocol parameters and over time have previously been evaluated, inter-institution reproducibility with PCCT remains unknown. PurposeThis study aimed to evaluate the repeatability and reproducibility of PCCT spectral results across four institutions using the same scanner model, phantom model, and protocol parameters. MethodsFour institutions scanned the same material inserts from the same multi-energy CT phantom model on the same PCCT model at a tube voltage of 140 kV and a volumetric dose index (CTDIvol) of 10 mGy. For all scans, virtual monoenergetic images (VMI) from 40 to 190 keV, iodine maps, and virtual non-contrast maps (VNC) were analyzed to determine the mean error relative to the expected value for each insert, spectral result, phantom copy, and institution. For all spectral results, the standard deviation across phantom copies and institutions ({sigma}ip) was calculated for each material insert to highlight variation from both phantom copies and institutions. Additionally, repeatability (RC) and reproducibility coefficients (RDC) were determined. ResultsAs VMI energy increased, quantitative variation between institutions decreased and stabilized. At VMI 70 keV, the {sigma}ip was 1.3, 3.8, and 2.7 HU for the blood 70, adipose, and iodine 5 mg/mL, respectively. The {sigma}ip increased to 7.4 HU at VMI 50 keV and decreased to 1.5 HU at VMI 150 keV. Similarly, the RDC for the iodine 5 mg/mL insert decreased from 20.6 to 4.1 HU as VMI energy increased from 50 to 150 keV. Iodine maps and VNC also exhibited reproducibility across the four institutions with RDC ranging from 0.08 to 0.49 mg/mL and 3.5 to 10.9 HU, respectively, across inserts. ConclusionThis multi-institutional study evaluated the variation of PCCT across a range of inserts and spectral results and demonstrated decreasing variation with increasing VMI energy levels. The characterized repeatability and reproducibility not only further reinforce the benefits of PCCT to support clinical translation and adoption but also provide guidance to ensure generalizable and clinically useful biomarkers for a range of clinical applications.

papers.title: Atlas-Based MRI Spatial Phenotyping in Pediatric Low-Grade Glioma
papers.abstract: Pediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGGs) arise throughout the developing brain, and their anatomic distribution is related to age, molecular subtype, and extent of resection (EOR). In clinical studies, pLGG location is commonly represented by a single manually assigned anatomic category, which does not quantify the full spatial extent of tumors spanning multiple brain regions. We developed and evaluated a reproducible, publicly available pediatric atlas-based framework integrating voxel-wise probabilistic mapping with patient-level atlas-derived spatial features. In this retrospective study, preoperative MRI from 349 patients with pLGG was registered to the Haskins pediatric template using EasyReg. Probabilistic maps showed differences in tumor distribution by age, molecular subtype, and EOR, including greater optic pathway and suprasellar involvement at 0-2 years and greater cerebellar involvement in KIAA1549-BRAF fusion tumors. Atlas-derived spatial, tumor morphometric, and clinical features distinguished gross total resection/near total resection from subtotal resection or biopsy/no-surgery (Replication area under the curve, 0.864). Substituting 107 automatically computed regional overlap features for the manually assigned location variable in previously published clinico-imaging risk stratification models did not significantly alter discrimination (smallest P = 0.12). Together, these group- and patient-level analyses demonstrate the frameworks utility for quantitative spatial phenotyping in imaging and clinical studies of pLGG.

papers.title: Sex-specific skeletal ageing trajectories and reference centiles across vertebrae and ribs in over 78,000 patients
papers.abstract: Skeletal aging is usually assessed at one site, so how bone loss differs across the skeleton and between sexes is unclear. We analyzed non-contrast torso CT from 2024 in 78,620 patients aged 15-100 years (41,056 men, 37,564 women) at nine Japanese hospitals, measuring mean attenuation of 25 vertebrae and 24 ribs from TotalSegmentator masks. We fitted sex-specific mean curves and quantile-regression centiles, and assessed each site as an L1 surrogate by age-adjusted correlation, errors-in-variables conversion and discrimination of low-for-age L1. Attenuation fell with age at all 49 sites in women and 46 of 49 in men, with a sex-dependent shape everywhere (all FDR-adjusted P < 0.0001). Female decline was steepest at a median of 52.0 years. L2 reproduced L1 closely (limits of agreement {+/-}45-46 HU); ribs did not ({+/-}68 to {+/-}82 HU). These centiles place an automated measurement at any of 49 sites against age- and sex-matched peers.

papers.title: Lesion selection and external evaluation of clinical-imaging survival models after transarterial chemoembolization for hepatocellular carcinoma
papers.abstract: BackgroundPretreatment computed tomography (CT) describes tumor characteristics in patients receiving transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but whether measuring more tumors improves mortality predictions in a new cohort remains unclear. We assessed the added value of different lesion-selection scopes beyond shared clinical predictors. MethodsWe compared a model using five clinical variables with models adding CT measurements from the largest, two largest, or all retained annotated tumors. All models used the same regularized discrete-time survival estimator. Evaluation used repeated nested cross-validation in 228 WAW-TACE patients and frozen external application in 69 HCC-TACE-Seg patients, with 15 deaths by day 365. We assessed first-year probability error, discrimination, and calibration, followed by local recalibration using small external samples. ResultsInternally, adding CT-derived lesion features did not establish an improvement in prediction accuracy. Externally, the all-lesion model had the highest discrimination point estimates, but its advantage over the clinical-only model was uncertain. Its mortality probabilities were less accurate than those of the clinical-only model, with calibration estimates consistent with overly extreme predicted risks. Local recalibration reduced its median held-out prediction error at day 365, but the median adjusted error remained higher than that of the adjusted clinical model. Simple tumor-burden predictors also did not improve external probability accuracy over the clinical baseline. ConclusionsIn these cohorts, measurements from more annotated tumors did not yield more reliable first-year mortality probabilities. Comparisons of clinical-imaging models should evaluate external probability accuracy and calibration alongside patient ranking.

papers.title: Fractional tumor burden refines prognostic stratification beyond MGMT status in glioblastoma after chemoradiotherapy
papers.abstract: Background and PurposeFollowing standard-of-care treatment for glioblastoma, response to chemoradiotherapy is difficult to evaluate because changes on postcontrast T1WI may represent either treatment effect or tumor progression, particularly in the early posttreatment period. Although O6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase promoter methylation is prognostic and informs treatment response, outcomes among patients remain heterogeneous. We hypothesized that combining advanced physiologic imaging with methylation status would improve early prognostic stratification. Materials and Methods.In this retrospective cohort study, patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma who underwent surgical resection or biopsy followed by standard chemoradiotherapy and had diffusion- and perfusion-weighted MR imaging within 6 weeks after treatment completion were included. Imaging-derived metrics included mean apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), mean standardized relative cerebral blood volume (sRCBV), change in contrast-enhancing volume on dT1, and the volume of fractional tumor burden (FTB), which is the volume of enhancing tissue with moderate-to-high probability of vascular tumor. Overall survival was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank testing. ResultsForty-three patients (21 male, 22 female) were included with a mean age of 57 years. Median overall survival was longer in patients with O6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase-methylated tumors compared with unmethylated tumors (19.7 vs 10.6 months; P = .01). Stratification by mean sRCBV, mean ADC, or change in dT1 volumes was not associated with overall survival (P > .05 for all comparisons). Among unmethylated tumors, FTB <5 mL was associated with longer overall survival compared with [≥]5 mL (14.5 vs 8.4 months; P = .006), whereas no survival difference, based on FTB volumes, was observed in methylated tumors (P = .50). ConclusionsFractional tumor burden, measured within 6 weeks after chemoradiotherapy, refines prognostic stratification beyond methylation status in glioblastoma, identifying a subgroup of unmethylated tumors with longer overall survival. These findings support the use of spatially resolved perfusion imaging to improve interpretation of early posttreatment enhancement.

papers.title: MedMLX: On-Device Medical Imaging AI for Apple Silicon
papers.abstract: BackgroundMedical imaging research increasingly combines specialized artificial intelligence models for segmentation, detection, image synthesis and report generation. For three-dimensional CT and MRI, these workflows typically run on NVIDIA GPUs with substantial memory. On-device AI on widely available Apple Silicon computers could broaden access to these models for clinical researchers. These computers share a large memory pool between the CPU and GPU, which suits workflows that combine several models. However, few established imaging models run natively on Apple Silicon. Adapting a model to new hardware also requires verifying that its results match the original software. MethodsWe developed MedMLX, a collection of 21 established medical imaging models rewritten for Apple Silicon in MLX, Apples machine learning framework. The collection includes nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, MedSAM2 and SAM 3. The models segment organs and tumors, detect lung nodules, generate synthetic images and draft radiology reports from CT, MRI, PET/CT, radiographs and endoscopic images. Using public cases from 11 imaging datasets, we compared the models results with those of the original software run on an Intel CPU and an NVIDIA GPU. Agreement required a Dice coefficient of at least 0.99 for every segmentation label and equivalent criteria for other outputs. We measured memory use and processing time on an Apple M1 Max computer with 64 GB of memory. ResultsMedMLX agreed with the original software in 211 of 212 comparisons. The single exception was a brain MRI segmentation. On this case, the original software itself gave different results on the two devices. We illustrated sequential workflows, including anatomical segmentation of a synthetic brain MRI and lesion synthesis guided by organ segmentation. With a memory-saving setting, 19 of the 21 models used less than 16 GB of memory. This setting reduced memory use by a median of 49% and increased processing time by a median of 13%. ConclusionsMedMLX enables on-device AI with established medical imaging models on Apple Silicon computers rather than specialized NVIDIA hardware. The models agree closely with the original software, and most need less than 16 GB of memory.

papers.title: Development and evaluation of automated organ segmentation models for abdominal ultrasound in injured children
papers.abstract: BackgroundAccurate organ segmentation in pediatric focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST) is an important prerequisite for automated image analysis and image quality assessment, but manual segmentation is time-intensive, subject to inter- and intra-observer variability, and limits the scalability of deep learning dataset development. Although deep learning has shown promise for ultrasound organ segmentation, its application to pediatric FAST has not been evaluated. ObjectiveTo describe the development and evaluation of deep learning models to automatically localize and segment six abdominal organs in pediatric FAST. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study using a convenience sample of archived FAST examinations from 200 injured children evaluated at a Level I pediatric trauma center. Emergency ultrasound fellowship-trained physicians manually segmented six key abdominal organs. Annotated image-mask pairs were split into training and test sets in an 80:20 ratio. We developed or fine-tuned U-Net, EVIT U-Net, UltraSAM, and nnU-Net models to automatically segment the bladder, kidney, liver, spleen, spine, and diaphragm. Segmentation accuracy was assessed using the Dice-Sorensen Coefficient (DSC) compared with manual annotations. Pediatric emergency ultrasound experts reviewed previously unlabeled FAST clips and rated the acceptability of model-generated organ masks. ResultsThe dataset included 1,807 manually annotated image-mask pairs from 200 pediatric FAST clips. Using an 80:20 split with no overlap between video clips, 1,446 image-mask pairs were used for training and 361 for testing. Across all models and organs, mean DSC was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.75-0.84). Mean DSC was highest for the kidney and bladder, each 0.91 (95% CI: 0.87-0.95), and lowest for the diaphragm at 0.63 (95% CI: 0.60-0.67). EVIT U-Net achieved the highest DSC for kidney, liver, and spleen, performed comparably to the highest-performing models for bladder, and had a mean inference time of 54 milliseconds per image. In previously unlabeled pediatric FAST clips, experts rated model-generated organ masks as acceptable for localization in 73%-95% of clips across organs. ConclusionWe describe the automatic segmentation of key abdominal organs in pediatric FAST with limited annotated data. This represents an important advancement in our image processing pipeline and can accelerate the development of large, robust datasets with segmentation for anatomy and pathology. Experts found that model-generated masks provided acceptable localization in most previously unlabeled pediatric clips, supporting the potential use of automated segmentation in pediatric FAST image analysis.

papers.title: Biopsy-Validated Deep Learning Mapping of Glioma Infiltration Beyond Contrast Enhancement Using Multiparametric MRI
papers.abstract: BackgroundGlioblastoma (GBM) exhibits diffuse tumor infiltration beyond contrast-enhancing margins into FLAIR-hyperintense brain tissue, where infiltrative tumor is not visible on conventional MRI. We developed and validated the infiltrative Tumor Burden (iTB) map, a deep learning biomarker that uses multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) to identify infiltrative tumor within these non-enhancing regions. MethodsPreoperative mpMRI datasets from 80 patients with WHO grade II-IV gliomas and 24 patients with brain metastases were retrospectively analyzed. Imaging included pre- and post-contrast T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion and diffusion MRI-derived maps (rCBV, rCBF, ADC). Spatially localized stereotactic biopsies from non-enhancing glioma regions provided histopathologic ground truth while peritumoral brain metastasis regions served as biologically grounded non-tumor controls. A 3D convolutional neural network was trained on voxel-centered mpMRI patches using patient-level cross-validation and an independent test set, with data augmentation optimized using a greedy local search strategy. ResultsModel development included 121 biopsy-localized samples from 56 glioma patients and 104 non-tumor samples from 26 brain metastasis patients. Augmentation optimization significantly improved independent test-set performance, increasing accuracy from 74.5% to 85.5% and AUC from 0.859 to 0.942 (p = 0.008). Ensemble-derived voxel-wise iTB maps demonstrated low infiltration probabilities in brain metastases and extensive regions of elevated infiltration probability in glioblastoma, consistent with expected biology. ConclusionsThe iTB biomarker generates voxel-wise maps of tumor infiltration within non-enhancing FLAIR abnormalities. Validated against image-localized histopathology and independent testing, it achieved high diagnostic performance and may improve surgical planning, radiotherapy targeting, and assessment of glioma burden.

papers.title: Divergence from Diffusion Tensor: a discriminant diffusion marker from single shell MRI
papers.abstract: PurposeThe Divergence from the Diffusion Tensor (DDT) is a new diffusion MRI metric that quantifies how the measured diffusion signal separates from the tensor assumption. It is marker for tissue heterogeneity that is estimated from single-shell data and can be used in brain studies. MethodsThere exist other techniques that allow the calculation of how the measured diffusion diverges from the Gaussian and tensor assumptions. However, the calculation requires large data-sets with different b-values, which makes them incompatible which standard diffusion tensor acquisitions. By imposing an initial assumption, an alternative formulation based on one single shell (ie, single b-value) is reported. ResultsPublicly available databases are used to test the behavior of DDT against other anisotropy measures. It shows the ability to discriminate different non-Gaussian diffusion scenarios with very low intra-subject variabilities. ConclusionsDDT can extract relevant information from the white matter, without any additional demands on data acquisition and totally compatible with standard diffusion MRI analysis pipelines. This makes DDT a good candidate to be used as an imaging marker for brain studies.

papers.title: Motion-robust high-resolution 3D-GRASE pseudo-continuous ASL perfusion imaging at 3T
papers.abstract: PurposeHigh resolution arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based perfusion imaging is desirable for many applications but suffers from low SNR and motion sensitivity due to the necessity for highly segmented readouts. Acquisition and reconstruction strategies were optimized for motionrobust high-resolution pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL) of the brain at 3T using segmented 3D Gradient and Spin Echo (3D-GRASE) at 2.0-mm isotropic resolution. MethodsA high-resolution 3D-GRASE pCASL sequence was implemented at 3T and evaluated with a focus on the interaction between background suppression strength and motion-corrected reconstruction, together with the fat suppression and control-tag subtraction strategies that strong suppression requires. Motion correction was performed using a novel motion-compensated (alignedSENSE-based) reconstruction that simultaneously estimates the motion and image, accounting for contrast changes between tag and control data. Eight healthy volunteers were scanned under motion-free and cued motion conditions. Image quality was assessed against motion-free reference images using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and a structural similarity index measure (SSIM). ResultsThe optimized acquisition-reconstruction pipeline enabled robust 2.0-mm isotropic pCASL at 3T and showed improved resistance to motion-related degradation. Strong BGS provided near-complete suppression of static tissue, and water excitation reduced lipid contamination and improved coil sensitivity estimation. The regularized alignedSENSE motion correction further improved perfusion-image quality, increasing SSIM by 18.7% under Strong BGS. ConclusionRobust high-resolution pCASL at 3T can be achieved through combined optimization of acquisition and reconstruction. The combination of Strong BGS, water excitation, reference-superimposed processing, and regularized motion correction mitigates motion-related degradation and yields higher-quality perfusion images for high-resolution ASL.

papers.title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD
papers.abstract: Foundation models have driven major advancements in the language and vision domains, as seen in the popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, and a growing number of studies are bringing the approach to human brain imaging. Whether these models are ready for independent researchers to use on clinical datasets has yet to be examined. We evaluated two recent fMRI foundation models, BrainLM and BrainHarmonix, on PreventAD, a dataset on adults with a family history of Alzheimers disease. We compared features from frozen and fine-tuned models against two baselines: functional connectivity and a dummy classifier that always predicts the most common class. The sample includes 343 subjects who passed quality control, with a subset of 218 who had amyloid PET imaging. We tested four prediction targets: sex, age, progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and {beta}-amyloid burden. Both models required substantial changes to the released code. BrainLMs own data preparation workflow did not produce stable fine-tuning, which we achieved only after switching to a standard workflow implemented with the library Nilearn. BrainHarmonixs documentation did not specify how to normalize new data, so we resolved this by testing different alternatives. For sex, functional connectivity outperformed all foundation model features. For age group, the best foundation model feature, taken from BrainHarmonixs structural (T1-weighted) encoder, slightly exceeded functional connectivity, but the difference was not significant. For MCI and {beta}-amyloid, no feature exceeded the dummy classifier in accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) stayed near chance for all features. For both clinical targets, the most precise feature came from fine-tuned BrainLM, meaning a larger share of its positive predictions were correct than for functional connectivity, but neither difference reached statistical significance. These results suggested that the strong transfer to new tasks seen in large language models cannot yet be assumed for fMRI foundation models, and that both models required code adaptation that would preclude their streamlined adoption by independent groups. We recommend that future studies provide standardized data workflows and always report functional connectivity and dummy classifier baselines. For clinical targets with strong class imbalance, studies should report several metrics, including precision.

papers.title: Training-free generation of 4D CT and other rare acquisitions improves segmentation across modalities
papers.abstract: RationaleRoutine clinical imaging captures anatomy under a limited set of physiologic and acquisition conditions, leaving segmentation models with sparse examples of how lesions and surrounding tissues deform with compression, respiration, or vascular pulsation. Standard image augmentation expands training datasets but does not explicitly model the mechanics underlying these changes. Patient-specific biomechanical simulation offers an approach to generate anatomically consistent images and corresponding segmentation masks under conditions absent from the original scan, without additional imaging or training a generative model. We hypothesized that incorporating this mechanistically grounded variability into training improves segmentation across imaging modalities. MethodsWe evaluate across three segmentation tasks: breast cancer on 3D digital breast tomosynthesis, lung tumors on chest CT, and carotid plaque on ultrasound. From each routine scan, patient-specific biomechanical models generate acquisitions absent from the original study--a range of breast compressions, the respiratory cycle, and arterial wall distension across the cardiac cycle. The resulting displacement fields deform both images and masks. Segmentation models were trained with and without the generated data across a range of standard image augmentation techniques, evaluated via cross-validation and held-out test sets. Realism was assessed through blinded reader studies, and generated respiratory motion was validated against real 4D CT. ResultsTraining on the generated acquisitions improved segmentation across modalities, increasing Dice scores by 6.6% for breast (p 0.05) relative to the routine scans alone. Generated respiratory motion closely matched real gated 4D CT, with Dice of 0.94 {+/-} 0.02 for lung volume overlap. Blinded readers discriminated generated from real images at near chance (AUC: breast 0.61, lung 0.41, carotid 0.46). ConclusionsMechanistic simulation generates imaging acquisitions that clinical systems do not supply, without training data or additional scanning, and improves AI-based disease detection across modalities.

papers.title: Usability and Physician Acceptance of AI in Chest Radiography: An Evaluation of the MeDeep Platform Using SUS and ATRAI-14
papers.abstract: ObjectivesArtificial intelligence (AI) architectures demonstrate high proficiency in chest radiography interpretation, yet successful clinical integration is often hampered by usability challenges and physician skepticism. This study evaluates the ergonomic usability and professional acceptance of the MeDeep AI platform among medical practitioners to identify key drivers of clinical trust. MethodsA multicenter, cross-sectional study was conducted across hospitals in Kermanshah, evaluating 88 medical professionals, including attending radiologists, radiology residents, internal medicine physicians, and medical externs. The System Usability Scale (SUS) was utilized to measure the platforms ergonomic functionality (n = 82), while the validated ATRAI-14 questionnaire quantified broader attitudes and trust regarding AI integration (n = 88). ResultsThe MeDeep platform achieved a high mean SUS score of 84.93, indicating excellent usability uniformly experienced across all professional subgroups (p = 0.387). However, overarching AI acceptance and algorithmic trust varied significantly by clinical role. Radiology residents exhibited significantly higher overarching AI acceptance (p = 0.016) and algorithmic trust (p = 0.008) compared to attending radiologists. Multivariate regression demonstrated that user familiarity (Beta = 0.500, p < 0.001) and perceived system usability (Beta = 0.236, p = 0.012)--rather than years of clinical experience--were the primary independent positive predictors of AI acceptance. Furthermore, higher perceived usability directly predicted greater algorithmic trust (Beta = 0.282, p = 0.009). ConclusionWhile technical usability is a necessary baseline for diagnostic platforms, professional trust dictates ultimate clinical adoption. Overcoming the generational divide in AI acceptance requires developers to prioritize intuitive interface design and position AI as a workflow-augmenting tool that addresses administrative burdens. Key PointsO_LIThe MeDeep AI platform demonstrated excellent ergonomic usability uniformly across all professional clinical ranks. C_LIO_LISignificant generational divides exist, with residents exhibiting higher algorithmic trust than attending radiologists. C_LIO_LIUser familiarity and perceived usability predict overarching AI acceptance better than years of clinical experience. C_LI

papers.title: Quantized TotalSegmentator for Fast Abdominal Organ Segmentation on CPUs
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDTotalSegmentator is designed for a graphics processing unit (GPU), runs slowly on a central processing unit (CPU), and depends on Python, limiting CPU-only clinical deployment. OBJECTIVEThe purpose of this study was to evaluate whether TS-Portable, a self-contained CPU executable running 8-bit integer (INT8)-quantized TotalSegmentator models, is noninferior to the reference implementation across 15 abdominal organs in an external multicenter cohort, quantify CPU-only runtime, and demonstrate spleen volumetry on a picture archiving and communication system (PACS) reading station. METHODSThis retrospective study compared TS-Portable with the reference Python implementation on 100 external multicenter CT scans and 28 chronic liver disease series. Per-case mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 3-mm normalized surface distance (NSD@3 mm) across 15 organs (1.5-mm resolution) and spleen-only mode were tested against a 0.01 noninferiority margin (paired bootstrap 95% CIs). Workstation and PACS runtimes were recorded; spleen volumes were compared via Lins concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) and Bland-Altman analysis. RESULTSThe external cohort included 100 patients (53 men, 47 women; mean age, 53 {+/-} 16 [SD] years). Across 15 organs, TS-Portable was noninferior for mean DSC (difference, 0.00017; 95% CI, 0.00003-0.00031; p < .001) and NSD@3 mm (difference, 0.00015; 95% CI, -0.00002 to 0.00031; p < .001) and in spleen-only mode (both p < .001). Workstation 1.5-mm median runtime was 48.0 seconds for TS-Portable on CPU versus 342.5 seconds on CPU (ratio, 7.14) and 61.5 seconds on GPU (ratio, 1.28) for the reference. On PACS, CPU spleen volumetry took 5.8 versus 43.4 seconds, agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.9999; bias, 0.2%; 95% limits of agreement, -7.2% to 7.6%) and manual contours (CCC, 0.989; bias, -6.8%). In 28 chronic liver disease series, TS-Portable ran from DICOM in 6.5 seconds (median), agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.99999) and manual contours (CCC, 0.992; bias, -3.4%). CONCLUSIONTS-Portable achieved noninferior abdominal organ segmentation accuracy compared with the reference implementation while running faster on a workstation CPU than the reference on a GPU. CLINICAL IMPACTSelf-contained deployment enables fast multiorgan segmentation on CPU-only computers and spleen volumetry within seconds on a standard reading station, without dedicated GPUs or software installation. HighlightsO_ST_ABSKey FindingC_ST_ABSAcross 100 external multicenter CT examinations, a quantized, self-contained CPU executable of TotalSegmentator was noninferior to the reference implementation for 15-organ segmentation accuracy and 7.14-fold faster on a workstation CPU, and completed reading-station spleen volumetry in a median of 5.8 seconds. ImportanceCompiling and quantizing three-dimensional segmentation models into a standalone CPU executable removes GPU and software-installation barriers, enabling rapid quantitative CT analysis on standard clinical workstations.

papers.title: Fine-tuned Medical Vision-Language Model (MedGemma 1.5 4B) with and without Structured Radiologist Descriptors versus EU-TIRADS for Malignancy Risk Stratification of Thyroid Nodules at Ultrasound: A Tunisian Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
papers.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate a medical vision-language foundation model fine-tuned on thyroid ultrasound images, with or without the radiologists structured descriptors, against expert-rated EU-TIRADS for the classification of thyroid nodules as benign or malignant. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study included nodules that underwent ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) between January 2019 and August 2025 in two Tunisian centers, with consecutive recruitment, together with a selection of images from an international public dataset. Of 1,580 nodules, 1,456 (272 malignant; 1,280 patients) with an interpretable cytological or histological reference standard were allocated at patient level to training (n = 942), validation (n = 258) and a test set sealed before training (n = 256; 51 malignant). MedGemma 1.5 4B was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation under four input configurations: the image with nodule biometry, with or without age and sex (A, B); A with chain-of-thought supervision (C); and A plus the eleven qualitative descriptors of the radiologists structured report (D). The EU-TIRADS category was never a model input. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were compared with DeLongs test and a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05; EU-TIRADS [≥] 4 was the prespecified comparator, with [≥] 5 as a sensitivity analysis. ResultsConfig D reached an AUROC of 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976), versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS (difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), which met the non-inferiority criterion; Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS). At [≥] 4, EU-TIRADS had a sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; at a threshold fixed on validation data, Config D reclassified 72 of them as negative while missing two additional cancers. Against EU-TIRADS [≥] 5 (sensitivity 92.2%, specificity 95.1%), Config D at its native threshold (88.2%, 94.1%) did not classify more nodules correctly (McNemar p = 0.22), and at its two other thresholds it classified fewer nodules correctly (p = 0.004 and 0.007). Raw probabilities were miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.117 for Config D), and Platt scaling within the test set reduced this error to 0.019-0.040. ConclusionGiven the ultrasound image together with the radiologists structured descriptors, the fine-tuned model matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination and, against the [≥] 4 threshold, reclassified most false positives as negative, a gain concentrated in category 4 and based on only three cancers in category 4. It is best positioned as a report-standardizing second reader in the EU-TIRADS 4 gray zone, pending prospective external validation. Summary StatementA fine-tuned medical vision-language model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists structured report matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination of thyroid nodules and would have deferred most aspirations of benign category 4 nodules, at the cost of one or two missed category 4 cancers depending on the threshold, based on only three cancers in category 4. Key PointsO_LIOn a test set of 256 thyroid nodules sealed before training, the model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists 16-field structured report reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.953, non-inferior to expert EU-TIRADS (0.948). C_LIO_LIAgainst EU-TIRADS 4 or higher, the model reclassified as negative 72 of the 94 false-positive nodules at a threshold fixed on validation data, at the cost of two additional missed cancers. C_LIO_LIAdding the radiologists qualitative descriptors to the image raised the area under the curve from 0.892 (Config A) to 0.953, and Platt scaling reduced the calibration error of the model from 0.117 to 0.019-0.040. C_LI

papers.title: Feasibility study on using the diffusion-weighted imaging liver pulsation artifact as marker of liver fibrosis
papers.abstract: BackgroundLiver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often shows signal loss in the left lobe due to cardiac pulsation, known as the pulsation artifact. PurposeThis study was conducted to turn this bug into a feature. We hypothesized that the pulsation artifact, caused by mechanically transmitted waves, is influenced by tissue stiffness and, thereby, indicative of cirrhosis in the left liver lobe. Thus, we evaluated the potential of DWI pulsation artifacts to detect liver cirrhosis. Study typeThis study included both retrospective patients and prospective healthy volunteers. Study populationThirteen healthy volunteers, 16 patients with cirrhosis (Ishak 5 or 6), and three patients without cirrhosis (Ishak 0, 1, or 2) were included. Field Strength/SequenceImaging was performed at 1.5 T and 3 T using echoplanar DWI of the liver with two b-values, b50 = 50 s/mm{superscript 2} and b800 = 800 s/mm{superscript 2}. AssessmentAfter manual segmentation of the left and right liver lobes, 18 first-order features were extracted from b50 and b800 images. We assumed the pulsation artifact was predominantly present in the left liver lobe in the b800 images. Thus, we computed the ratios of the intensity-normalized b800 features obtained from the left and right liver lobes. Additionally, we performed an intensity normalization to address the sometimes different signal intensities of left and right liver lobe. Then, we conducted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers. Statistical testsROC analysis and leave-one-out bootstrapping were applied, both yielding area under the curve (AUC) values. ResultsLeft liver pulsation artifacts were more pronounced in non-cirrhotic livers and largely absent in cirrhotic livers. The first quartile feature, i.e. the first quartile of the normalized signal, best distinguished cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers (AUC = 0.95; 95% confidence interval 0.87 - 1.00). Data conclusionThe left liver DWI pulsation artifact reflects liver stiffness and could serve as a simple, intrinsic marker of liver cirrhosis. Analysis of the signal magnitude can differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers.

papers.title: Ordinal Multi-Instance Learning for Automated Multi-Task Grading of Lumbar Degenerative Conditions on Sagittal MRI, with External Validation
papers.abstract: PurposeLumbar spine MRI interpretation requires 25 structured severity judgments per examination -- five degenerative conditions at five disc levels, each on a three-level ordinal scale -- a time-consuming task with substantial inter-reader variability. We developed and externally validated a model that automates this complete scheme. Materials and MethodsA full-sequence multi-instance learning (MIL) model -- ResNet34 backbone, bidirectional GRU, attention pooling over 24 uniformly sampled sagittal T2-weighted slices -- with 25 cumulative-logit ordinal heads was trained on 1,204 examinations from the multi-institutional RSNA 2024 LumbarDISC dataset and internally validated on 213 held-out examinations. External validation used 60 retrospectively collected patients from an independent Chinese university hospital (four scanner vendors, radiology reports as the reference standard, no fine-tuning). Agreement was assessed with exact accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, McNemar tests, and patient-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. ResultsThe ordinal model achieved 51.4% balanced accuracy internally (exact accuracy 65.1%), versus 16.3% for a single-slice baseline; severe-grade AUCs averaged 0.908 across conditions. Externally, it outperformed its softmax-weighted counterpart on exact accuracy (0.649 vs. 0.586; +6.3 percentage points, 95% CI +2.7 to +10.0) and sensitivity (0.868 vs. 0.833), with markedly fewer severe-grade false alarms (69 vs. 172 predicted severe cells; McNemar p<0.0001). ConclusionA full-sequence MIL model with ordinal outputs automates the complete 25-task grading scheme on sagittal MRI and, in the first hospital external validation of such a model, reduced severe-grade over-prediction under domain shift without loss of sensitivity -- supporting its role as a screening and triage aid. SummaryAn ordinal full-sequence multi-instance learning model graded all 25 lumbar MRI degeneration tasks and markedly reduced severe-grade false alarms in 60-patient hospital validation without loss of sensitivity. Key PointsO_LIFull-sequence attention was indispensable: balanced accuracy rose from 16.3% (single-slice baseline) to 51.4% over 24 sagittal slices. C_LIO_LIIn external validation, ordinal outputs reduced severe-grade predictions from 172 to 69 of 900 cells (McNemar p<0.0001) with comparable ranking ability (AUC 0.835 vs. 0.829). C_LIO_LIThe Moderate grade remained the hardest class across all conditions (AUC 0.70-0.78), tracking known inter-reader variability at the mild-moderate boundary. C_LI

papers.title: Structural damage of the cervical spinal cord within and beyond the maximal compression area in mucopolysaccharidosis types I and VI
papers.abstract: BackgroundCervical spinal cord (CSC) compression and myelopathy are frequent, severe complications in mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) types I and VI. Early detection is critical to prevent irreversible neurological deficits and preserve quality of life. This prospective study aimed to identify quantitative neuroimaging biomarkers of structural CSC damage and myelopathy in MPS I and VI. MethodsStructural and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the CSC was analyzed in 17 MPS I patients, 3 MPS VI patients (19{+/-}7 years), and 19 case-matched healthy controls (20{+/-}7 years). CSC macrostructure (cross-sectional area, diameters) and microstructure (fractional anisotropy [FA], radial [RD], mean, axial diffusivities) were evaluated within and beyond the maximal compression areas. ResultsMPS patients demonstrated reduced CSC cross-sectional area and anterior-posterior diameter at upper cervical levels, alongside widespread microstructural alterations (lower FA, higher RD) throughout the CSC versus controls (pFDR<0.05). Restricted foramen magnum space was associated with microstructural damage at lower cervical levels without overt macrostructural compression. Morphological and microstructural metrics were sensitive to CSC compression and myelopathy severity (pFDR<0.05). Lower CSC integrity correlated with more advanced growth retardation (p<0.001). Among patients receiving hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, earlier treatment correlated with preserved upper CSC morphology (p<0.05). Distinct neuroimaging phenotypes were observed across MPS genotypes (pFDR<0.05). ConclusionsCSC MRI provides candidate neuroimaging biomarkers for early detection and characterization of myelopathy in MPS I and VI. Structural damage extends beyond primary maximal compression areas, highlighting these markers for clinical monitoring and future therapeutic trials.

papers.title: Discrepancies in Interpretation of Japanese Radiology Report Expressions Between Radiologists and Referring Physicians
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo evaluate discrepancies between radiologists and referring physicians in the interpretation of diagnostic probabilities conveyed by common Japanese expressions used in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsFifteen expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities in radiology reports were selected by five attending radiologists. An anonymous online survey was distributed to 26 radiologists and 33 referring physicians at a single institution. Participants assigned a diagnostic probability (from 0% to 100% in 10% increments) to each expression. Differences in median probabilities between radiologists and referring physicians were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Variability in interpretation was assessed using interquartile range (IQR), with IQR [≥] 30% defined as substantial variability. ResultsAll radiologists (26/26) and 97% of referring physicians (32/33) completed the survey. Seven of the 15 expressions showed statistically significant differences in interpretation between radiologists and referring physicians: "c/w" (80% vs. 60%; p = 0.031), the Japanese equivalents of "present" (100% vs. 100%; p = 0.024), "suspect of" (80% vs. 70%; p = 0.007), "possibly" (50% vs. 70%; p < 0.001), "unlikely" (10% vs. 10%; p = 0.022), "cannot be ruled out" (25% vs. 40%; p < 0.001), and "not inconsistent with" (80% vs. 90%; p = 0.008). Substantial variability in interpretation (IQR [≥] 30%) was observed for four expressions: "cannot be ruled out" (IQR, 10%-40%), "s/o" (IQR, 60%-90%), "c/w" (IQR, 50%-90%), and "not inconsistent with" (IQR, 70%-100%). ConclusionThis study revealed that nearly half of the Japanese expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities were interpreted differently by radiologists and referring physicians. These discrepancies highlight the need for a standardized lexicon to improve clarity and consistency in radiology reporting. Compliance with Reporting GuidelinesThis study was conducted in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational studies.

papers.title: Disagreement between AI and Radiologists: Quantifying Direction and Fragility
papers.abstract: BackgroundConventional performance metrics do not indicate whether artificial intelligence (AI)-platforms and radiologists are right or wrong on the same examinations, nor whether their non-agreement is more often beneficial or harmful. ObjectiveTo develop, illustrate, and apply directional metrics quantifying non-agreement between radiologists and AI-platforms against a common reference standard, and to adapt a fragility-based framework for quantifying the statistical robustness of these metrics. MethodsWe defined Positive Non-Agreement (PNA, AI-platform correct, radiologist incorrect), Negative Non-Agreement (NNA, radiologist correct, AI-platform incorrect), and Net Non-Agreement (NENA, their difference). Metrics were illustrated in three hypothetical scenarios of 1,000 examinations each and applied to three previously published AI-radiologist studies on pulmonary embolism and mammography. Bootstrap confidence intervals were calculated, and a reclassification fragility index (FI) quantified the minimum case reclassification needed to remove statistical support for NENAs direction. ResultsIn illustration, NENA was positive in two scenarios and negative in one. In the three published studies, NENA ranged from -4.18% to +10.74% and decreased consistently with increasing radiologist experience (junior residents, +6.27%; consultants, +1.45%), a gradient driven primarily by declining PNA with modest increase in NNA. The reclassification FI was defined for all three illustrative scenarios (range, 0.10%-1.70%) and for six of the seven comparisons from these studies (range, 0.34%-4.31%), but not for the weakest comparison, whose confidence interval for NENA included zero. ConclusionsPNA, NNA, and NENA provide a directional, case-level complement to conventional performance metrics for AI-radiologist non-agreement. The accompanying reclassification FI offers a statistically grounded, generalizable method for quantifying their robustness. Summary SentencePositive, Negative, and Net Non-Agreement, directional metrics developed and applied to published datasets comparing artificial intelligence with radiologists, show that the net benefit of artificial intelligence assistance depends on reader experience and clinical setting, and that the statistical robustness of these directional conclusions varies by comparison and sample size, which is information that conventional performance metrics alone do not provide. Key Points- Positive Non-Agreement (PNA), Negative Non-Agreement (NNA), and Net Non-Agreement (NENA) are directional metrics that identify whether AI-radiologist non-agreement is more likely to be beneficial or harmful, complementing conventional performance metrics to inform AI validation and monitoring decisions. - The reclassification fragility index (FI), anchored to statistical significance rather than to the point estimate, quantifies how many case reclassifications would remove support for the direction of NENA. - Applied to three previously published AI-radiologist datasets NENA ranged from -4.18% to +10.74% and fell from +6.27% to +1.45% with increasing radiologist experience, a gradient driven primarily by declining PNA with modest increase in NNA.

papers.title: Scaled m-BonacciNet: A Recurrence-Guided Lightweight CNN for Efficient Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: The m-Bonacci weighted sequence space [Formula] is introduced for m [≥]2, 1[≤]p 0. It is proved to be a Banach space isometrically isomorphic to lp, with an unconditional Schauder basis. The space is also reflexive and uniformly convex. Its strict inclusion chain, continuous dual, and asymptotic truncation estimate of order[Formula] are established. Based on this framework, Scaled m-BonacciNet is proposed as a lightweight CNN that rescales Fibonacci-Net channels using the dominant m-Bonacci root and employs depthwise separable convolutions. Tribonacci-Net achieved 96.09% accuracy and 0.9581 macro F1-score on the 15-class Brain MRI dataset using 0.85 million parameters and 0.366 GFLOPs. Pentanacci-Net attained 95.87% accuracy on the 44-class dataset, reducing parameters and FLOPs by 47.10% and 44.48%. Hexanacci-Net achieved 83.75% accuracy and 0.7941 macro F1-score on CKD ultrasound.

papers.title: Morphometric Brain Networks at Ultra-Low Field: A First Assessment of Feasibility and Reliability
papers.abstract: Ultra-low field (ULF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers accessible point-of-care neuroimaging, yet its capability to support multivariate network analyses remains understudied. We systematically evaluated the feasibility and reliability of Morphometric Similarity Networks (MSN) and Morphometric Inverse Divergence (MIND) networks derived from paired high-field (HF, 3T/1.5T) and ULF (64mT) scans in a primary cohort(N=23) and an independent replication cohort (N=19). We tested the impact of super-resolution processing, cortical parcellation granularity (Desikan-Killiany vs. Destrieux), and mesh resolution (fsnative vs. fsaverage5) on edge-level cross-scanner agreement (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, CCC) and subject-level identifiability. MIND networks demonstrated higher edge-level HF-ULF agreement (mean CCC = 0.95) and ULF reproducibility (mean CCC = 0.98) compared to MSNs (mean CCC = 0.86-0.87 and 0.91-0.94, respectively). In contrast, MSNs yielded higher subject-level differential identifiability across field strengths due to a broader distinction between within- and between-subject similarity. Reconstructing MIND networks on native high-resolution meshes (fsnative) maximised cross-scanner agreement, whereas coarser meshes and finer cortical parcellations enhanced individual network identifiability. Structural similarity networks can be reliably constructed from ULF MRI data. Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.
